items.label: Crucifixion of Jesus
items.note: Jesus is crucified under Pontius Pilate; scholarship places the date in AD 30 or 33.

items.label: Paul's conversion
items.note: Paul's Damascus-road experience, generally dated one to three years after the crucifixion.

items.label: Council of Jerusalem
items.note: Apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem over the terms of Gentile inclusion (Acts 15).

items.label: Great fire of Rome; Nero's persecution
items.note: After the great fire, Tacitus reports that Nero punished Christians in the city of Rome.

items.label: Fall of Jerusalem
items.note: Roman forces under Titus take Jerusalem and destroy the temple.

items.label: Reign of Domitian (traditional persecution)
items.note: Domitian's reign, traditionally associated with pressure on Christians toward its end.

items.label: Pliny-Trajan correspondence
items.note: Pliny, governing Bithynia, asks Trajan how to handle accused Christians, and Trajan replies.

items.label: Bar Kokhba revolt
items.note: The Bar Kokhba revolt in Judea ends with Jerusalem refounded as a Roman colony.

items.label: Martyrdom of Polycarp
items.note: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, is executed in the city's stadium; the date is placed between 155 and 160.

items.label: Death of Justin Martyr
items.note: Justin Martyr is executed in Rome under the prefect Junius Rusticus, c. 165.

items.label: Paul's undisputed letters
items.note: The seven letters whose Pauline authorship is undisputed are dated to roughly 50-58.

items.label: Gospel of Mark
items.note: Most scholars date the earliest gospel to the years around the Jewish War, 65-75.

items.label: Gospels of Matthew & Luke
items.note: Matthew and Luke are generally dated after Mark, within the range 75-95.

items.label: Gospel of John
items.note: The fourth gospel is commonly dated to the range 90-110.

items.label: Revelation
items.note: Revelation is most often dated near the end of Domitian's reign, c. 95.

items.label: The Book of Enoch (1 Enoch)
items.note: Composed in stages across the third–first centuries BC. Jude quotes it by name; the Ethiopian church receives it as scripture.

items.label: The Didache
items.note: A church manual of the Two Ways, baptism, and eucharist, dated anywhere from the mid-first to the early second century.

items.label: Gospel of Thomas sayings tradition
items.note: The sayings tradition behind Thomas is dated anywhere from c. 60 to 140, with the surviving form usually placed in the second century.

items.label: The Epistle of Barnabas
items.note: An anonymous letter reading the Jewish law as an allegory of Christ; dated between the fall of the Temple (70) and Hadrian's reign, with no consensus within that span.

items.label: Ascension of Isaiah
items.note: A composite apocalypse — the Martyrdom of Isaiah joined to the Vision of the Beloved's descent through seven heavens; its parts span the late first and early second centuries.

items.label: Shepherd of Hermas
items.note: An apocalyptic work of visions and parables from Rome, composed in stages between c. 90 and 150.

items.label: 1 Clement
items.note: The Roman church's letter to a divided Corinth, traditionally dated c. 95-96 near the end of Domitian's reign.

items.label: Ignatius' seven letters
items.note: Seven letters written under guard on the road to martyrdom in Rome, traditionally dated c. 107-110 under Trajan.

items.label: Fragments of Papias
items.note: Papias' five books on the sayings of the Lord, written in the early second century and now lost; the surviving fragments include the earliest account of how Mark and Matthew were composed.

items.label: Polycarp to the Philippians
items.note: Polycarp's letter to the church at Philippi; proposed dates run from shortly after Ignatius' journey to c. 140.

items.label: 2 Clement
items.note: The earliest surviving Christian sermon, wrongly ascribed to Clement; commonly dated to the mid-second century. Its ending was recovered only in 1873.

items.label: Epistula Apostolorum
items.note: A dialogue of the risen Christ with the apostles; scholars date it across the second century, c. 120–170.

items.label: Fragment of Quadratus
items.note: The oldest Christian apology, presented to the emperor Hadrian around 124; a single sentence survives, quoted by Eusebius.

items.label: Epistle to Diognetus
items.note: An anonymous apology of uncertain date, estimates running from the early second century to c. 200; shown here at its earlier bound.

items.label: The Martyrdom of Polycarp
items.note: The Smyrnaean church's account of Polycarp's death, written soon after the events it describes.

items.label: Third Corinthians
items.note: The apocryphal correspondence between the Corinthian church and Paul, part of the Acts of Paul; Paul's reply defends the resurrection of the flesh against teachers who denied it.

items.label: The Abgar Correspondence
items.note: Eusebius records a legendary exchange between King Abgar of Edessa and Jesus; the correspondence as we have it is generally dated to the early fourth century.

items.label: The Apocalypse of Paul
items.note: Paul's tour of heaven and hell in a late-fourth-century apocalypse — a major source behind later visions of the afterlife, including Dante.
